issue: Source: 'The consciousness of good intentions disdains ambiguity.' Candidate: 'A conscience clear of bad intentions disdains ambiguity.' Changes the claim from positive good intentions to absence of bad ones.
replacement: In these observations, my fellow-citizens, I have meant to put you on your guard against every attempt, from whatever quarter, to sway your decision on a matter of the utmost importance to your welfare by any impressions other than those that come from the evidence of truth. You will no doubt also have gathered, from the general drift of what I have said, that it comes from a source not unfriendly to the new Constitution. Yes, my countrymen, I own to you that, having given it careful consideration, I am clearly of the opinion that it is in your interest to adopt it. I am convinced that this is the safest course for your liberty, your dignity, and your happiness. I do not claim a reserve that I do not feel. I will not entertain you with a show of deliberation when I have already decided. I frankly tell you my convictions, and I will freely lay before you the reasons on which they rest. A consciousness of good intentions disdains ambiguity. I shall not, however, multiply professions on this point. My motives must stay in the keeping of my own breast. My arguments will be open to all, and may be judged by all. They shall at least be offered in a spirit that will not disgrace the cause of truth.

issue: Source: 'although town or country, or other contracted influence'. Candidate silently repairs to 'Town or county influence'. A probable misprint must stay as the source reads (open issue).
replacement: First, once an effective national government is established, the best men in the country will not only be willing to serve but will generally be the ones chosen to run it. Town or country influence, or some other narrow influence, may put men into State assemblies, senates, courts of justice, or executive departments. But offices under the national government will require a wider and more extensive reputation for talents and other qualifications. This is especially so because the national government will have the widest field to choose from and will never suffer the shortage of suitable persons that is not uncommon in some of the States. It will follow that the administration, the political counsels, and the judicial decisions of the national government will be wiser, more systematic, and more judicious than those of the individual States. They will therefore be more satisfactory to other nations, and more SAFE for us.

issue: Source 'their Doge, or chief magistrate'. Candidate 'chief executive' is within the STYLE-NOTE table but the table's parenthetical covers the President/governors; 'chief official' is a safer neutral rendering for a Genoese Doge. Optional.
replacement: In 1685 the state of Genoa, having offended Louis XIV, tried to appease him. He demanded that they send their Doge, or chief official, accompanied by four of their senators, to FRANCE, to ask his pardon and receive his terms. For the sake of peace they had to submit. Would he ever have demanded or accepted the same humiliation from Spain, or Britain, or any other POWERFUL nation?

issue: Source emphasis 'forbearing to give JUST causes of war'; candidate 'avoiding just causes' drops the capitals (STYLE-NOTE: keep emphasis capitals). Source 'JUST' is paired with 'PRETENDED' in the next sentence.
replacement: But the safety of the people of America against dangers from FOREIGN force depends on more than their avoiding JUST causes of war. It also depends on their placing and keeping themselves in a position that does not INVITE hostility or insult. I hardly need point out that there are PRETENDED causes of war as well as just ones.

issue: (a) Source 'absolute monarchs will often make war when their nations are to get nothing'; candidate 'will even make war' drops 'often'. (b) Source 'to aggrandize or support their particular families'; candidate 'to enrich or support' narrows 'aggrandize' (advance/enlarge) to wealth only.
replacement: It is only too true, however shameful to human nature, that nations in general will make war whenever they see something to gain by it. Absolute monarchs will often make war when their nations stand to gain nothing, for purely personal ends: a thirst for military glory, revenge for a personal insult, ambition, or private agreements to advance or support their own families or partisans. These motives and many others touch only the mind of the sovereign, and they often lead him into wars that justice does not sanction and his people neither want nor benefit from. These inducements are more common in absolute monarchies, but they deserve our attention. Apart from them, however, there are others that move nations as often as kings, and some of them, as we shall see, grow out of our own situation and circumstances.

issue: Source 'when the fleets of America may engage attention'; candidate 'will draw attention' strengthens the modal.
replacement: We have heard much about the fleets of Britain, and the time may come, if we are wise, when the fleets of America may draw attention. But suppose one national government had not regulated British navigation so as to make it a nursery for seamen. Suppose one national government had not called forth all the national means and materials for building fleets. Then British prowess and British thunder would never have been celebrated. Let England have its navigation and fleet, and Scotland its own, and Wales its own, and Ireland its own. Let those four constituent parts of the British empire live under four independent governments, and it is easy to see how soon each would shrink into comparative insignificance.

issue: Source 'flattered into neutrality by its specious promises'. Candidate 'attractive promises' loses the sense of deceptive plausibility that the argument needs.
replacement: Apply these facts to our own case. Suppose America left divided into thirteen independent governments, or, if you like, three or four. What armies could they raise and pay? What fleets could they ever hope to have? If one were attacked, would the others rush to its aid and spend their blood and money in its defense? Would there be no danger that they would be flattered into neutrality by its deceptively attractive promises? Or that they would be seduced by too great a love of peace into refusing to risk their tranquillity and present safety for the sake of neighbors whom they have perhaps been jealous of, and whose importance they are content to see reduced? Such conduct would not be wise, but it would be natural. The history of the states of Greece, and of other countries, is full of such instances, and it is not unlikely that what has so often happened would happen again in similar circumstances.

issue: Source 'The history of Great Britain is the one with which we are in general the best acquainted'; candidate 'We know the history of Great Britain better than that of any other country' drops the qualifier 'in general'.
replacement: In general we know the history of Great Britain better than that of any other country, and it teaches many useful lessons. We can profit from their experience without paying what it cost them. Common sense says that the people of such an island should be one nation. Yet for ages they were divided into three, and those three were almost constantly caught up in quarrels and wars with one another. Their true interest with respect to the nations of the Continent was in fact the same. Even so, the arts, policy and practices of those nations kept their mutual jealousies burning without pause. For a long series of years they were far more of a nuisance and a trouble to each other than a help and support.

issue: Source 'different degrees of political attachment to and connection with different foreign nations'; candidate drops 'and connection with'.
replacement: When did the independent states into which Britain and Spain were once divided join in such an alliance, or combine their forces against a foreign enemy? The proposed confederacies will be DISTINCT NATIONS. Each would have its own commerce with foreigners to regulate by its own treaties. Their products and commodities differ and suit different markets, so those treaties would be essentially different. Different commercial concerns must create different interests and, naturally, different degrees of political attachment to and connection with different foreign nations. It might therefore happen, and probably would, that the foreign nation the SOUTHERN confederacy was at war with would be the very one with which the NORTHERN confederacy was most anxious to keep peace and friendship. An alliance so contrary to their immediate interest would not be easy to form. If it were formed, it would not be kept and fulfilled in perfect good faith.

issue: Source ends with a rhetorical question ('How many conquests did the Romans and others make in the characters of allies, and what innovations did they ... introduce ...?'); candidate turns it into two statements. STYLE-NOTE: keep the rhetorical questions.
replacement: It is far more probable, in fact, that in America as in Europe, neighboring nations would be driven by opposite interests and unfriendly passions and would often be found on different sides. Given our distance from Europe, it would be more natural for these confederacies to fear danger from one another than from distant nations. Each would therefore be more eager to guard against the others with the help of foreign alliances than to guard against foreign dangers with alliances among themselves. And here let us remember how much easier it is to let foreign fleets into our ports and foreign armies into our country than to persuade or force them to leave. How many conquests did the Romans and others make while posing as allies, and what changes did they introduce, in the same character, into the governments of those they pretended to protect?

issue: Source 'Let candid men judge'; candidate 'fair-minded readers' changes the referent from men to readers.
replacement: Let fair-minded people decide, then, whether splitting America into any number of independent sovereignties would protect us from the hostilities and the improper meddling of foreign nations.

issue: Source 'are topics that have been too often descanted upon not to be generally known'; candidate 'to need telling here' replaces the claim (generally known) with an authorial aside.
replacement: The influence that the bigotry of one woman,(6) the petulance of another,(7) and the cabals of a third(8) had on the policy, the ferments, and the pacifications of a considerable part of Europe in their time has been discussed too often not to be generally known.

issue: Source 'till it was relinquished in the treaty of peace' (passive, no agent). Candidate 'until he gave it up' supplies an agent (the king).
replacement: Territorial disputes have always been among the most fertile sources of hostility among nations. Perhaps the greatest share of the wars that have desolated the earth sprang from this origin. This cause would exist among us in full force. We have a vast tract of unsettled territory within the boundaries of the United States. Several of the States still have discordant and undecided claims against each other, and the dissolution of the Union would lay a foundation for similar claims among them all. It is well known that they have already had serious and heated discussion over the rights to the lands that were ungranted at the time of the Revolution, and that usually went by the name of crown lands. The States within whose colonial boundaries those lands lay have claimed them as their property. The other States have argued that the rights of the crown in this matter passed to the Union. They argue this especially for all that part of the Western territory which, by actual possession or through the submission of the Indian proprietors, was under the jurisdiction of the king of Great Britain until it was given up in the treaty of peace. This, it has been said, was in any event an acquisition to the Confederacy by compact with a foreign power. Congress has prudently tried to calm this controversy by persuading the States to make cessions to the United States for the benefit of the whole. This has been accomplished far enough to give a decided prospect, if the Union continues, of a friendly end to the dispute. A breakup of the Confederacy, however, would revive the dispute and would create others on the same subject. At present a large part of the vacant Western territory is the common property of the Union, by cession at least, if not by any earlier right. If the Union were ended, the States that made the cession on a principle of federal compromise would be apt to claim the lands back as a reversion once the motive for the grant had ceased. The other States would no doubt insist on a proportion, by right of representation. Their argument would be that a grant, once made, could not be revoked, and that the justice of sharing in territory won or secured by the joint efforts of the Confederacy remained as strong as ever. Suppose, against probability, that all the States admitted that each had a right to a share of this common stock. There would still be a difficulty to overcome in finding a proper rule of apportionment. Different States would put forward different principles for the purpose, and since these would touch the opposing interests of the parties, they might not easily be settled peacefully.

issue: 'pernicious' rendered 'destructive' and then 'destructive contentions' repeats the word two sentences apart; 'Their view' has an unclear referent (the preceding papers).
replacement: The probability that different States or confederacies would form incompatible alliances with different foreign nations, and the effects of this situation on the peace of the whole, have been sufficiently set out in some earlier papers. The view they have given of this part of the subject leads to this conclusion: if America were not connected at all, or only by the feeble tie of a simple league, offensive and defensive, such clashing alliances would gradually entangle her in all the harmful labyrinths of European politics and wars. The destructive contentions of the parts into which she was divided would likely make her a prey to the artifices and machinations of powers that were equally the enemies of them all. Divide et impera(1) must be the motto of every nation that either hates or fears us.(2)
